text:
Jules: Quick help — HearthBank POC is Monday. They want a Private deployment in their AWS account. Need concise checklist: PrivateLink vs VPC peering recommendation, firewall ports + FQDN/IPs for allowlisting, egress IP preservation (we need client's allowlist), and rough delta on pricing: hosted via PrivateLink vs Private deployment on-prem. Also need answers for security questionnaire items: data at rest, KMS, logging. PTAL @Nate @Priya

Nate: +1. High-level: prefer PrivateLink for cross-account minimal routing complexity. Peering can work but has transitive limitations and requires route tables + more ops. PrivateLink = interface endpoints to our service LB in customer VPC (ENIs) — preserves customer egress IPs to external services; our traffic originates from customer subnets. Use PrivateLink if they cannot allow inbound peering or want stronger isolation.

Priya: Quick bullets for their network team:
- Outbound: customer instances -> our interface endpoint (PrivateLink). Ports: 443 only (TLS).
- If they prefer NAT egress to our hosted endpoint: allow outbound 443 to these hostnames: api.redwood-inference.{region}.amazonaws.com and embeddings.redwood-inference.{region}.amazonaws.com
- If using VPC Peering: require route table entries for the subnets that will talk to our service; security groups must allow HTTPS from app subnets to service subnets.

Sam: Firewall snippet (pasteable):
```
# Allow outbound to PrivateLink endpoint
Type: OUTBOUND
Protocol: TCP
Port: 443
Destination: vpce-<vpce-id>.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com OR ENI IPs created by the VPC endpoint

# Allow outbound to hosted API (if peered/proxy)
Destination hostnames: api.redwood-inference.prod.{region}.svc (CNAME to A/ALIAS)
```
Note: ENI IPs are allocated by AWS and can change; better to allow by FQDN or use customer egress proxy with preserved source IP.

Arun: Security answers (short):
- Data at rest: Customer model data and request logs are encrypted at rest using KMS (customer-managed CMKs available for Private deployments).
- Key management: Supports AWS KMS and HSM integrations in Private. For hosted we use provider-managed keys unless customer requests CMK.
- Logging: We stream audit and access logs to customer CloudWatch/S3 in Private deployments. For hosted API, we provide redacted request logs and can push audit events to customer SIEM via secure webhook on enterprise plans.

Emma: Pricing delta (very rough for customer-facing):
- Hosted + PrivateLink: usage-based metered billing + PrivateLink data processing fee (per-GB) + support SLA addon. Lower up-front but variable.
- Private deployment (customer VPC / on-prem): platform license + monthly reserved capacity (for dedicated GPU pools) + integration/setup fee. Higher commitment but predictable unit costs for high throughput.
I can follow up with exact numbers once we know expected TPS and token rates. :moneybag:

Jules: They asked about source IP preservation for allowlisting — if we use PrivateLink, the traffic appears to come from their own VPC (ENIs) so no extra allowlist needed. If they NAT through a corporate proxy, they'll need to provide static egress IPs or set up an NAT GW.

Nate: One more operational note: for POC, recommend spinning up a small test subnet and provision a VPCE (interface) in that AZ, then test curl from an EC2 in their app subnet:
```
curl -v https://vpce-<id>.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com/health -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
```
If TCP resets or TLS handshake issues occur check SGs/NACL for port 443 and MTU settings.

Priya: Can someone draft two one-paragraph replies for the SOC/security team and the network team? I can send them to the customer.

Arun: I'll drop quick text for the SOC: 'Redwood supports encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+), at-rest encryption with KMS, role-based access controls, audit logging, and customer-managed keys for Private deployments. We can provide SOC2 / ISO artifacts via the secure portal upon NDA.' Keep it short.

Sam: Network paragraph: 'Recommended deployment: PrivateLink interface endpoints in your VPC. Allow outbound HTTPS (443) from app subnets to the endpoint. For peering, add route entries and allow HTTPS between subnets. Avoid CIDR overlap. If allowlisting is required upstream, provide static egress IPs or use NAT Gateway.'

Jules: Awesome. I'll send both and ask for their expected TPS/token volume so Emma can price.
